pages.text: A volcano is an opening in the earth's crust through which molten rock, ash, and gas escape from deep inside the planet. Volcanoes can be gentle, releasing slow lava flows that creep across the landscape for weeks. They can be catastrophic, exploding with a force that flattens forests, collapses mountains, and changes the climate of the entire earth. They are among the most powerful forces in nature.

image.note: Illustration: cross-section of a volcano showing magma chamber, conduit, crater, and lava flow

pages.text: The earth beneath our feet is not solid. The outermost layer, the crust, is a relatively thin shell of rock ranging from about five kilometres thick under the oceans to about 70 kilometres thick under mountain ranges. Beneath the crust is the mantle, a layer of rock so hot that it behaves almost like a very thick liquid, flowing extremely slowly over millions of years. Below the mantle is the core: iron and nickel, the outer part liquid, the inner part solid.

Volcanoes form where the crust is weak or where one section of crust is pushing beneath another. The vast majority of the world's volcanoes are found in a zone called the Ring of Fire, which encircles the Pacific Ocean. Others form at mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates are pulling apart and magma rises to fill the gap. A few form over hot spots, places where an unusually hot section of the mantle melts through the crust from below.

The ground you stand on floats. The earth's hard shell is cracked into vast slabs called tectonic plates, drifting on the hot, slow-flowing rock beneath at about the speed your fingernails grow. Where plates pull apart, dive under one another, or grind past, the earth's fury escapes: volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain ranges. Nearly every volcano on the planet sits on a plate boundary, which is why they line up in chains around the world.
Not all volcanoes look the same or behave the same. Their shape and behaviour are determined by the type of magma they contain.

Shield volcanoes have gently sloping sides and produce runny lava that flows easily and travels long distances before cooling. They build up slowly into broad, low-profile mountains. The Hawaiian islands are shield volcanoes. Their eruptions are dramatic but relatively slow-moving and rarely kill people, because there is usually time to evacuate.

image.note: Comparison diagram: shield volcano (broad, low) vs stratovolcano (steep, narrow)

pages.text: Stratovolcanoes, also called composite volcanoes, have steep sides built from alternating layers of lava and ash from many previous eruptions. Their magma is thick and sticky, trapping gas bubbles. When the pressure becomes high enough, the gas explodes outward with enormous force. Stratovolcanoes produce the most violent eruptions. Vesuvius, which buried the Roman city of Pompeii in 79 CE, was a stratovolcano. Krakatoa, whose 1883 eruption was heard 4,800 kilometres away, was a stratovolcano.

Caldera volcanoes form when a volcano erupts so violently that it empties its magma chamber and the top of the mountain collapses inward, forming a huge depression called a caldera. Yellowstone in the United States sits above one of the largest caldera systems in the world. If it were to erupt, the consequences for North America and for global climate would be severe.

Not all lava is equal. Runny, low-silica lava flows like hot syrup, spreads far, and builds gentle shield volcanoes. Thick, sticky, high-silica magma traps gas until the pressure explodes, blasting out ash and rock. That is the difference between a Hawaiian eruption you can almost walk beside and a killing blast like Mount St Helens. Volcanologists can often predict a volcano's temper simply by testing the chemistry of what it erupts.

A supervolcano is a different order of danger. Beneath places like Yellowstone lie magma chambers so vast that a full eruption would bury half a continent in ash and cool the whole planet for years. Such eruptions are rare, tens of thousands of years apart, and none has occurred in human history. Scientists monitor these giants constantly. The point is not to frighten but to watch: an understood danger is a survivable one.

The eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE buried the Roman city of Pompeii under four to six metres of volcanic ash in less than a day. The ash preserved the city almost perfectly, entombing the bodies of those who did not escape in the exact positions in which they died. When archaeologists excavated the site in the eighteenth century, they found a city frozen in time: bakeries with bread still in the ovens, houses with furniture intact, people forever preserved in the last moment of their lives.

pages.text: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia was the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history. It ejected so much ash into the atmosphere that it blocked sunlight worldwide. The following year, 1816, became known as the Year Without a Summer. Crops failed across Europe and North America. Tens of thousands of people starved. The eruption and its aftermath killed more than 70,000 people in total.

In 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted after being dormant for 600 years. It was the second largest eruption of the twentieth century. Scientists from the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology monitored the mountain closely in the weeks before the eruption and were able to warn and evacuate most of the population at risk. An estimated 5,000 lives were saved. Volcanology, the science of volcanoes, can genuinely save lives.

Volcanoes shape more than mountains; they shape history. The eruption of Thera around 1600 BCE may have helped end the Minoan civilisation. Tambora's blast in 1815 stole a summer and caused famine across the world. Yet the same volcanoes lay down the richest farmland on earth and, deep underground, the heat that powers whole countries. Iceland and Kenya generate clean electricity from volcanic steam. Destruction and gift pour from the same vent.

Volcanic eruptions are destructive. They can also be creative. Lava cools to form new rock. Volcanic ash, which contains minerals in a fine, water-soluble form, produces some of the most fertile soil on earth. Communities have lived on the slopes of active volcanoes for centuries because the soil there grows extraordinary crops.

Many of the world's most productive agricultural regions sit on ancient volcanic soil. The hills around Naples in Italy. The slopes of Mount Etna in Sicily. The highlands of Rwanda and Ethiopia. The Central Valley of California. Volcanic islands like Java in Indonesia support some of the highest population densities on earth, because the volcanic soil allows dense food production.

Nigeria has no active volcanoes. The closest active volcanic system is the Cameroon Volcanic Line, which runs from the Gulf of Guinea into Cameroon and includes Mount Cameroon, the highest mountain in West Africa, which last erupted in 2000. The Benue Trough, which runs across central Nigeria, is a failed rift valley from the age when the African and South American continents were separating, and occasional minor seismic activity in Nigeria is related to this ancient geological history.

image.note: Map of West Africa showing Cameroon Volcanic Line and its proximity to Nigeria

pages.text: Understanding volcanoes is understanding the earth. The forces that produce volcanoes, the slow movement of tectonic plates, the heat of the mantle, the chemistry of magma, are the same forces that built the continents, raised the mountain ranges, and shaped every landscape on earth. Volcanoes are a window into a planet that is still, after 4.5 billion years, very much alive.

Nigeria sits far from the world's violent plate boundaries, on a stable block of ancient crust, so it has no erupting volcanoes and few strong earthquakes. But the story reaches its border. The Cameroon Volcanic Line, running from the Gulf of Guinea into Cameroon, includes Mount Cameroon, West Africa's highest peak, which last erupted in 2000. And the ancient volcanic rocks of the Jos Plateau remind Nigerians that even a quiet land was, long ago, shaped by fire.
